# Achieving Reproducibility: Perspectives and New Tools {.unnumbered}

{{< include "../includes/WIP-callout.qmd" >}}

This resource is drawn from a talk on computational reproducibility in MRI
research, built around experience running the Stanford Center for Cognitive
and Neurobiological Imaging (CNI) and developing the Flywheel data and
computation platform. The talk's own summary of the argument is a simple
chain: quantitative measurements feed computational models, and both must be
built so that they can be checked and shared
(@fig-repro-title-triangle-summary).

![Quantitative measurements, computational models, and the discipline of
checking and sharing — the throughline of this
talk.](images/reproducibility/title-triangle-summary.png){#fig-repro-title-triangle-summary}

**Disclosure.** The presenter is an active participant in Flywheel Exchange
LLC, a commercial venture related to the data-management platform described
here. The story begins with work at Stanford building a new MRI neuroimaging
center, and that work was later transferred to Flywheel as a commercial
venture.

## Motivation: a reproducibility problem with two different causes

Much of the public conversation about reproducibility in neuroscience and
psychology focuses on statistical reproducibility — whether *N* is large
enough, whether *p* is small enough, whether the right test was used, or, in
the worst cases, outright research misconduct (fabricated or manipulated
images have been the basis of several recent high-profile retractions and
investigations, as documented in books such as *Bad Blood* by John Carreyrou
and *Rigor Mortis* by Richard Harris). But for a center that manages MRI data
for many labs, a different and more tractable problem is at least as
important: computational reproducibility — whether the specific chain of
software, parameters, and data versions that produced a given result can be
recovered and rerun at all, independent of whether the underlying statistics
were sound. Replication (repeating an experiment to see if the scientific
finding holds up) and computational reproducibility (recovering the exact
computational pipeline behind a result) are related but distinct goals, and
an MRI center is much better positioned to guarantee the second than the
first, since replicating expensive, complex MRI experiments is not
something a data-management platform can solve on its own.

Computational reproducibility is not something that can be bolted on after
the fact. It has to be designed into a project from the beginning, with a set
of programming and research disciplines that are maintained throughout the
project's life. Large, well-funded projects like the Human Connectome
Project (HCP) and the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) study
have this discipline built in — but the argument here is that every lab
should have access to it, not just the largest consortia.

## From simple beginnings to a data-management problem

In the early 1990s, MRI acquisition was comparatively simple, and there was
correspondingly little need — or ability — to do much in the way of data
management; computational infrastructure and data-analysis methods were
primitive by later standards (@fig-repro-mri-room-1992). By the time a new
MRI center for cognitive and neurobiological imaging was being built roughly
fifteen years later, in 2008, both the instrumentation and the computational
demands had grown substantially more complex, and Stanford's own IT
infrastructure could not, by itself, solve the data-management problem that
running a modern multi-user MRI center creates (@fig-repro-cni-construction-2008).

![MRI acquisition in 1992: simpler hardware, and correspondingly limited
computational infrastructure for data
management.](images/reproducibility/mri-room-1992.png){#fig-repro-mri-room-1992}

![Building the Stanford Center for Cognitive and Neurobiological Imaging
(CNI) in 2008 raised data-management questions that the scanner hardware
alone could not
answer.](images/reproducibility/cni-construction-2008.png){#fig-repro-cni-construction-2008}

## Data management as a prerequisite to computational reproducibility

The starting point is architectural: data should be archived at the center
itself, before it ever leaves, and made available through a platform-independent
web browser rather than requiring users to re-gather or manually copy their
own data for each analysis or publication
(@fig-repro-web-browser-database-access). Storing data thoughtfully at the
point of capture — rather than simply handing raw files out to whoever asks
— is treated here as close to a professional obligation, not a nicety.

![Archiving data at the center and exposing it through a platform-independent
web browser removes the burden on individual users to re-gather data for
publication or
re-analysis.](images/reproducibility/web-browser-database-access.png){#fig-repro-web-browser-database-access}

Underneath that browser-based access sits a data capture architecture that
has to classify and interpret many different kinds of MR data — raw DICOM
from the instrument or a hospital PACS system, legacy data users want to add
retroactively, behavioral and physiological recordings that matter for
reproducibility, and the output of custom reconstruction pipelines — and
route all of it, de-identified, into a per-project store
(@fig-repro-flywheel-data-capture-architecture).

![The Flywheel data capture architecture: a reaper process classifies,
de-identifies, and uploads many different MR and non-MR data types into a
user's
project.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-data-capture-architecture.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-data-capture-architecture}

## Tools are better than rules

A recurring lesson from running a multi-user center: it works better to give
users good tools than to try to enforce data-management rules by policy
alone. Users have different preferences for how they want to pre-process
their data, project membership changes over time so permissions need to be
easy to manage, and many users want help with pre-processing, project notes,
and visualization rather than being left to solve those problems themselves
(@fig-repro-flywheel-tools-better-than-rules).

![Tools, not just rules: gear rules, per-user permissions, and a built-in
image viewer, all attached directly to a
project.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-tools-better-than-rules.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-tools-better-than-rules}

In practice, this means packaging common computations as installable,
shareable units — called Gears in Flywheel — so that many kinds of analysis
can be installed once and shared between users. A single lab's site might
share dozens of Gears with collaborators, including FreeSurfer, FSL, HCP
pipelines, tractography tools, file-format converters (DICOM), and
directory-structure converters (BIDS), among others
(@fig-repro-flywheel-providing-users-tools). Every time a Gear runs, its
parameters are stored automatically in the project's provenance record, so
that exactly how a given result — a FreeSurfer run, for example — was
produced can always be recovered later
(@fig-repro-flywheel-gears-provenance).

![Gears package common analyses (FreeSurfer, FSL, HCP pipelines,
tractography, format conversion, and more) as installable, shareable
units.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-providing-users-tools.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-providing-users-tools}

![Computational record keeping: the Gears used and their parameters are
stored automatically in a project's Provenance
tab.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-gears-provenance.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-gears-provenance}

## Cloud-scale computing and programmatic access

"Cloud-scale" here means something specific: the ability to select and run
many Gears across many different data sets at the same time, with the cloud
provider handling the underlying machine provisioning on demand
(@fig-repro-flywheel-cloud-scale-computing). This matters because data sets
have grown larger and analyses more complex — capacity that would be
impractical for an individual lab to provision and maintain on its own.

![Cloud-scale computing: many Gears can be run across many data sets
simultaneously, with compute capacity provisioned on
demand.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-cloud-scale-computing.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-cloud-scale-computing}

Beyond pre-packaged Gears, programmers need to be able to write their own
special-purpose scripts and explore new methods. A software development kit
(SDK) exposes language bindings for Python, MATLAB, and R, along with REST
database endpoints, so that new computations can be developed and shared
just as easily as the pre-packaged ones
(@fig-repro-flywheel-sdk-language-bindings). In practice, this SDK can be
driven from a Jupyter notebook or a MATLAB Live Script to search for data,
download it, run an analysis such as a FreeSurfer segmentation, and upload
the resulting analysis back into the system — a complete round trip from
query to stored, reproducible result
(@fig-repro-flywheel-sdk-livescript-interface).

![Language bindings (SDK) for Python, MATLAB, and R, plus REST database
endpoints, support exploration and new methods
development.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-sdk-language-bindings.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-sdk-language-bindings}

![A MATLAB Live Script driving the SDK: search Flywheel for T1-weighted
files, download them, run a FreeSurfer segmentation, and upload the analysis
back to the
project.](images/reproducibility/flywheel-sdk-livescript-interface.png){#fig-repro-flywheel-sdk-livescript-interface}

## Databases built for different purposes

At the time of publication, curated data is often placed on a shared public
site such as OpenNeuro, the NIMH Data Archive (NDA), the USC Laboratory of
Neuro Imaging's Image and Data Archive (IDA), or FITBIR, among others (LORIS,
COINS, and XNAT serve similar roles). These sites add real value — checking
data quality and providing standard pipelines — but they are designed for a
different purpose than an MRI center's own data system: they are built to
host curated, published data for reuse, not to manage an ongoing project's
full range of cloud computation
(@fig-repro-shared-databases-comparison).

![Public data-sharing platforms (OpenNeuro, NDA, IDA, FITBIR) serve a
different purpose than a center's own data-management
system.](images/reproducibility/shared-databases-comparison.png){#fig-repro-shared-databases-comparison}

Statistical reproducibility is a related but separate concern from the
computational reproducibility this resource focuses on. Null-hypothesis
statistical testing and group comparisons remain deeply embedded in
neuroscience's publication culture, particularly in cognitive and clinical
neuroscience, and the NIH itself has published principles and guidelines for
reporting rigorous, reproducible preclinical research
(@nih-rigorreproducibility). The tools described here are built to support
many kinds of computation — not to adjudicate the final statistical
hypothesis test.

## FAIR principles

Flywheel's design is explicitly an attempt to implement the FAIR
principles — a set of community-developed guidelines stating that data (or
any digital object) should be Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and
Reusable (@wilkinson2016-fairprinciples). Computational reproducibility, in
this framing, is what it looks like to take the FAIR principles seriously in
the specific context of a working MRI center: measure quantitatively, build
computational models on top of those measurements, and build the whole
pipeline so that it can be checked and shared
(@fig-repro-fair-principles-nature-article).

![The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and
stewardship (@wilkinson2016-fairprinciples), the framework Flywheel is built
to
implement.](images/reproducibility/fair-principles-nature-article.png){#fig-repro-fair-principles-nature-article}
